title: Why input() Always Gives You Text, Even When You Type a Number
excerpt: Ask users for data with input(), then learn why every answer arrives as text and how to turn it into a number you can calculate with.

headings.text: Ask a Question and Keep the Answer
Convert the Answer With int() or float()
When the Answer Is Not a Number

html:
Most programs become useful the moment they can ask a question and react to the answer. In Python, the tool for that is input(), a ready-made command that comes with Python (programmers call such a command a function): it pauses the program, waits for the user to type something and press Enter, and hands you what they typed.

No matter what the user types, input() gives it back as text (a string), never as a number. That one fact causes the most common beginner error with input(), so this lesson shows the error on purpose and then fixes it.

In the examples below, the answers a user would type are shown right after each prompt, so you can see exactly what the program would display.

Ask a Question and Keep the Answer

You give input() a prompt, which is the message shown to the user, and store the result in a variable:

name = input("What is your name? ")
print("Hello,", name)
What is your name? Asha
Hello, Asha

The first line of the output is the prompt followed by the answer the user typed. The second line is what the program printed afterwards. How does Python know when the answer is finished? It waits for the Enter key; everything typed before it becomes the value.

The Answer Is Always Text

Now ask for an age, a value that is clearly a number:

age = input("How old are you? ")
print(age)
print(type(age))
How old are you? 41
41
<class 'str'>

The function type() reports what kind of value something is, and <class 'str'> means str, short for string, which is Python's word for text. The user typed digits, so why is the type text? Because input() cannot know what you plan to do with the answer. It might be a name, a phone number or a number you want to add. Python plays it safe and gives you the exact characters typed.

That safety turns into a bug the moment you try arithmetic:

print(age + 1)
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

Python refuses to add a number to text, because it cannot tell whether you wanted 42 or the text "411". The message calls this a TypeError, which means you used a value of the wrong kind for the operation; "concatenate" is the message's word for joining pieces of text.

Convert the Answer With int() or float()

Wrap the text in int() to get a whole number, or float() to get a number with decimals. Which one should you pick? Use int() for things like an age or a count, and float() when decimals are possible, such as a price:

age = int(age)
print(age + 1)
42

You can convert straight away, in a single line:

price = float(input("Price: "))
print(price * 2)
Price: 19.5
39.0

Read it from the inside out: input() runs first and returns text, then float() turns that text into a number, then the result is stored in price.

When the Answer Is Not a Number

What if the user types "forty" instead of "40"? Python cannot guess what you meant, so the conversion fails with an error:

int("forty")
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'forty'

The message calls this a ValueError: the text "forty" cannot be read as an ordinary whole number. A simple guard is a check called isdigit(). A method like this is a built-in action you attach to a piece of text with a dot, and isdigit() answers True or False (Python's two yes/no values), where True means every character is a digit. Check first, convert second:

answer = input("How many tickets? ")
print(answer.isdigit())
print("40".isdigit())
How many tickets? forty
False
True

A program can use that True or False to decide what to do next. Note that isdigit() rejects values such as 3.5 and -2, because the dot and the minus sign are not digits.

Putting It Together

Here is a complete tiny program that asks three questions and uses every idea from above:

name = input("Name: ")
first = int(input("First number: "))
second = int(input("Second number: "))

print(name, "your total is", first + second)
Name: Ravi
First number: 12
Second number: 30
Ravi your total is 42

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonInputFunction.ipynb.

Summary

  • input(prompt) shows the prompt, waits for Enter, and returns what was typed.
  • The returned value is always a string, even when the user types digits.
  • Adding a number to that string raises a TypeError.
  • Wrap the answer in int() or float() to calculate with it.
  • Converting text that is not a number raises a ValueError; check with isdigit() first if you cannot trust the input.
